transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Reed (PM - LatticeApps), Maya Singh (Staff Eng), Samir Patel (CTO)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Priya our solutions engineer. Quick agenda - we'll do a fast hosted API demo for chat gen, show streaming, params, and then dig into retry patterns and operational bits. Jordan: yep, sounds good.

[00:24] Priya: Cool, I'm going to share my screen and start with a simple chat request in the sandbox. This is using the Redwood hosted endpoint /v1/chat.generate (auto-transcript sometimes drops slashes). I'll send a short prompt and stream the output.

[00:45] Maya: Quick Q - we mostly care about 95th/99th percentile latency, and that partial responses don't become inconsistent when clients reconnect.

[01:05] Priya: Totally. For stream behavior, we emit incremental deltas as tokens are generated. On reconnects, you can attach an idempotency key and a resume-token - the client can request the last stable token index. We also recommend using short-lived prefix caching for repeated opening prompts to reduce cold-token cost. (audio: Priya says K-V cache, transcript reads K V cache.)

[01:42] Alex: I'll show parameters in the request: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, presence_penalty, and stop tokens. Example: temperature 0.2 for deterministic replies; 0.8 for more creative. Jordan: how do you recommend we set those for our support chat use case?

[02:05] Priya: For issue triage / support, lower temp (0.0-0.3) and top_p 0.9 usually. Use stop sequences to avoid trailing system prompts. Also set max_tokens to cap hallucination length. For multi-turn agents trim conversation history: use a token budget and summarize older turns - Redwood Console Optimize suggests summarization rules per route.

[02:38] Jordan: Got it. Cost concerns - how does streaming affect token count? Are partial tokens billed?

[02:52] Alex: Billing is per output token that the model emits plus input tokens. Streaming doesn't change billing - it's a transport mechanism. Batching and prefix caching reduce per-token cost by lowering repeated context. Also we have Optimize suggestions in Console that will flag high-cost prompts and recommend quantized model variants if latency budget permits.

[03:23] Samir: We run on mobile and web clients. What about idempotency for retries? If a user hits send twice we want to avoid duplicate actions.

[03:38] Priya: Two-pronged approach: attach an idempotency key per user-interaction server-side; for streaming disconnects, your client should checkpoint last token index and include that on reconnect. The runtime supports dedupe via request metadata and will return a dedup token. If you need strict exactly-once semantics, put the action behind your service with a unique request ID that you check server-side.

[04:05] Maya: Does Redwood provide client SDKs to simplify this?

[04:12] Alex: Yes, we have SDKs (JS, Python, Go). Priya will paste example code in slack after this; it includes streaming reconnect logic and idempotency key patterns.

[04:35] Priya: I'm going to run a demo of a simulated intermittent network. I'm sending a 500-token prompt and we'll intentionally kill the connection at ~200 tokens to show how the client can reconnect and resume. (screen noise)

[05:10] Priya: Disconnecting now... reconnecting... see the client asks for resume-token=tx123 and Redwood returns the buffer of confirmed segments. Minor note: sometimes transcripts say 'resume token' as 'resume tonne'.

[05:34] Jordan: In cases where we can't resume, do you recommend re-issuing the generation or trying to stitch partial outputs?

[05:50] Priya: If you have partial stable content, you can stitch with a new prompt that includes last confirmed chunk as context. If not, re-issue with the same idempotency key - Redwood will dedupe and return the existing response rather than generating again. For streaming the runtime uses short transaction TTLs for resumability to avoid holding KV cache indefinitely.

[06:22] Samir: Our privacy team will ask about logs and encryption. Where are the logs stored and can we KMS them?

[06:35] Alex: Hosted offers optional envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS for keys at rest. We keep audit logs and per-token usage traces for debugging but you can opt-in/out of retention windows. We'll share the SOC2 + KMS docs as requested.

[07:05] Priya: Back to parameters - small demo of temperature/top_p interplay. I'll send the same prompt with temp 0.0, 0.5, and 0.9. You'll see divergence in wording. Also mention of penalties - presence vs frequency - to discourage repetition.

[07:35] Alex: Another parameter: stop sequences. If your UI has a bot prefix like 'Assistant:', set stop to that label to prevent the model adding extra assistant tokens.

[08:02] Jordan: What about rate limits and retries under throttling? Do you recommend client-side exponential backoff?

[08:15] Priya: Yes, exponential backoff with jitter. For streaming we recommend graceful fallbacks: if you detect 429, back off and try route to a lower-cost model variant or queued request pattern. Redwood can do smart routing by policy - you can route by latency SLO or cost. Also discuss burst capacity for Dedicated customers - not relevant for hosted but good to know.

[08:50] Maya: Can we do a quick look at Console Optimize suggestions?

[08:55] Alex: Sure, switching to console. The Optimize panel flags prompts that exceed token thresholds, suggests batched calls for high-throughput patterns, and gives quantization recommendations if your throughput can tolerate slightly higher latencies. See the demo rule: it flagged a 1.2k prompt and suggested summarizing older turns.

[09:22] Jordan: Are those suggestions automated or do they require manual review?

[09:30] Priya: They are suggestions with short-circuit toggles. You can run an auto-apply in a dev sandbox, but changes need manual approval for production rollouts. There's also an eval framework to ensure quality hasn't regressed.

[09:50] Samir: For our SLA discussion later, what's your typical 95th percentile on hosted for a chat model at 512 tokens?

[10:05] Priya: Rough numbers on p95 for small-medium models are in the 120-220 ms per token range depending on region and sequence length; longer contexts increase kernel overhead. We'll put precise numbers from your region in the benchmark run.

[10:28] Alex: Now a quick walk-through of retry playbook patterns: 1) Client retries with idempotency key + exponential backoff; 2) If partial stream was delivered, request resume with resume-token; 3) If you must re-run, use dedupe on server with request-id. Also logging: attach request metadata so you can match requests to audit traces.

[11:10] Jordan: Any gotchas around streaming order or concurrency?

[11:20] Priya: If you parallelize multiple requests for the same conversation, be careful - race conditions can create inconsistent histories. We recommend serializing mutating operations per conversation or use vector of logical timestamps. Batching is great for throughput but not for strict turn order.

[11:45] Maya: We have a microservice that sends many short prompts. Would you recommend batching on the server or per-connection?

[11:55] Alex: Server-side batching is recommended for high throughput to reduce GPU kernel overhead. Redwood runtime does continuous batching across requests when configured, and Console Optimize can show batching benefits as estimated cost savings. For real-time chat with tight latency needs, keep batch windows small.

[12:20] Priya: I'm going to show a quick SDK snippet (JS) that demonstrates streaming reconnect + idempotency. I'll paste it in the follow-up Slack because screen text is small. The core idea: create a unique idempotency key per user message, checkpoint lastConfirmedTokenIndex periodically, and on reconnect request resume. This avoids duplicates.

[13:05] Jordan: What about function/tool calling for structured outputs - do retries affect side-effects?

[13:18] Priya: Yes, if you invoke an external action in the middle of generation, best practice is to have the model produce a discrete action payload that your service validates idempotently. Redwood supports function-calling patterns in the request payload.

[13:55] Samir: The transcription garbled the JSON snippet there, but we got the idea.

[14:05] Alex: We're nearing the hands-on part - Jordan, do you want sandbox credentials now or after the benchmark?

[14:12] Jordan: We want credentials now so our engineers can poke while Priya runs the benchmark. Also share a test script.

[14:20] Alex: Will do. We'll include three example requests: deterministic support reply, a creative summarization, and a long multi-turn chat.

[14:35] Priya: Quick note on failure modes - partial tokens on stream might arrive out of order to the client if the client buffers incorrectly. Always render in-order based on token index. If you store user-visible transcripts, persist confirmed segments, not transient buffers.

[14:58] Jordan: For retry policy, how long is the resume-token valid?

[15:05] Priya: Resume tokens are short-lived (couple minutes) by default to reduce KV cache pressure. For longer resumes we recommend saving the confirmed transcript and re-issuing with that context.

[15:28] Maya: Can Console show us per-route cost estimates before we push live?

[15:35] Alex: Yes, Console shows per-route token breakdown and cost estimates; you can simulate traffic and get an estimate. Optimize will also surface suggestions like model down-variant or quantization if cost is a problem.

[15:58] Jordan: Any final comments on security?

[16:05] Alex: Reiterate: hosted with customer-managed KMS integration, options for VPC peering for enterprise, SSO via SAML/SCIM, audit logs, and retention windows that you can configure. We'll send the security questionnaire link.

[16:30] Priya: OK let's recap next steps: send sandbox creds + playbook; run the benchmark; schedule deep dive on private deployment. Anyone object?

[16:40] Samir: Fine. Also can you include a sample contract term for data residency?

[16:48] Alex: Yes we'll include a sample clause and the legal contact.

[17:00] Jordan: Thanks, really useful demo. Priya: thanks for the reconnect demo - that helped.

[17:12] Alex: Great, we'll follow up with artifacts. Meeting ends.

Notes: transcription includes small recognition errors (JSON snippet garbled, KV vs K-V cache etc.). Links referenced during call: sandbox invite link (https://redwood.example/sandbox/invite/LA-guest) and security questionnaire (https://redwood.example/security/questionnaire). Priya promised to paste SDK snippets and the benchmark sheet into Slack and the CRM.
